name: Anti-globalization movement
summary: A loose network of movements opposing corporate-led globalization, as embodied in the WTO, IMF, World Bank and trade deals, which it says put profit above democracy, labor, the environment and local self-determination. Its mainstream wants democratic control of the economy, protection of commons and public services, debt cancellation and fair rules, and organizes through decentralized direct action and coalitions.
scope: The left, internationalist 'movement of movements' that surfaced at Seattle (1999) and met at the World Social Forum, as two of its leading voices describe it: Klein's account of many linked struggles against corporate-led globalization and privatization (s1), and Chomsky's view that the label is propaganda and that the movement favours globalization 'that attends to the rights of people' (s2). Both question the name: Klein asks whether it is really a movement or anti-globalization. It excludes the nationalist and Christian-right opponents of globalization that the bare label can also cover; the defining sources treat the movement as internationalist and egalitarian.

notes: The label covers both left internationalists and nationalist or Christian-right opponents of globalization; answers follow the left mainstream. Confidence is mostly low on social issues the movement never addressed. Some answers use sources read in summary only; PGA source s5 is cited for hallmarks but no answer relies solely on it. Rules-7 pass 2026-11-24: answers rebuilt from the defining sources tied in the scope phase (Klein, NLR 9; Chomsky, ZNet interview; Graeber, NLR 13 opening); 182 earlier answers resting on Wikipedia articles and inference were nulled with history. Themes searched: trade and globalization, privatization, democracy and organizing, labour, borders and nation, environment, debt. Klein's and Graeber's NLR texts are open only in part; the WSF Charter, PGA hallmarks and ATTAC pages could not be tied or fetched.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Klein presents colonialists telling indigenous peoples they must do things differently to 'develop' as part of what the movement resists.

corporate-influence.rationale: Klein counts 'politicians are bought and altered' among the harms the movement fights, and Graeber says power is being ceded to 'an elite of economists and corporate flacks'.

direct-action.rationale: Graeber says direct action rejects appeals to governments in favour of physical intervention, while Klein also describes proposals to turn the commons into law; neither says it should replace electoral politics.

experts-over-public.rationale: Graeber's complaint is that an elite of economists and corporate flacks holds power once held by democratically accountable institutions.

free-trade.rationale: Klein lists 'anti-free trade' among the movement's names and describes the fight against NAFTA and a hemispheric free trade area under 'The World is Not for Sale'; Graeber calls 'free trade' a propaganda term for neoliberalism; Chomsky says the 'free trade agreements' are investor-rights deals.

gm-crops.rationale: Klein lists genetically altered seeds among the harms of privatization and approves the destruction of Monsanto's test soya by Bové and the MST.

land-redistribution.rationale: Klein approvingly describes landless peasants and the MST occupying land to farm it.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Klein describes the movement's campaigns against privatizing water, health and education, with Bolivian workers reversing the privatization of their water supply and the call that water 'isn't a private good'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Graeber says the movement is against neoliberalism, 'market fundamentalism' (or 'market Stalinism'), and Klein objects to commodifying every activity and value.

nation-first.rationale: Klein reports the shift from defending a nation to a cause that 'transcends nationality and state borders', with local and national struggles seen through a global lens.

open-borders.rationale: Graeber defines the globalization the movement favours as the effacement of borders and free movement of people, possessions and ideas; Chomsky says no sane person opposes international integration.

unions-good.rationale: Klein names cross-border unionization and basic labour rights, and tells how farm workers with no bargaining power organized against Taco Bell; Chomsky says the workers' movements were founded on international solidarity.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Klein ties corporate wealth to the buying of politicians and the fight for democracy, and Chomsky objects to globalization as concentration of wealth and power.

workers-nation.rationale: Chomsky says the left and workers' movements were founded on the principle of international solidarity.
